For finite on-site loss $\gamma>0$ and finite on-site spin-flip amplitude $\Omega$, the spectrum and eigenstates of the tight-binding Hamiltonian
      $$

      H = & -t_{s}\sum_{\langle\vec{i},\vec{j}\rangle}\left(c_{\vec{i}\uparrow}^\dagger c_{\vec{j}\uparrow}-c_{\vec{i}\downarrow}^\dagger c_{\vec{j}\downarrow}\right)
      +\sum_{\vec{i}}\Gamma_z\left(n_{\vec{i}\uparrow}-n_{\vec{i}\downarrow}\right)\\
      & +\sum_{\vec{i}} t_{\mathrm{so}}\left(c_{\vec{i}\uparrow}^\dagger c_{\vec{i}+\mathbf{e}_x\downarrow}-c_{\vec{i}\uparrow}^\dagger c_{\vec{i}-\mathbf{e}_x\downarrow}\right)+\text{H.c.}\\

steps.reasoning: Take the tight-binding non-Hermitian lattice Hamiltonian $H$ (established previously) as the starting point for spectral and eigenstate analysis; consider finite on-site loss $\gamma>0$ and finite on-site spin-flip amplitude $\Omega$ as parameters that break Hermiticity and provide mechanisms for non-reciprocal bulk transport.

Compute numerically the complex eigenspectrum and the spatial distributions of eigenstates of $H$ under three different boundary conditions: (i) periodic boundary conditions (PBC) along both $x$ and $y$, (ii) periodic along $x$ but open along $y$, and (iii) open boundary conditions (OBC) along both $x$ and $y$. Use a finite square lattice (the authors show results for a $20\times20$ lattice) and parameter values $t_{\mathrm{so}}/t_s=1$, $\Gamma_z/t_s=1$, $\Omega/t_s=0.5$, and $\gamma/t_s=2$ for illustrative computations.
Fig. 2

Report the observed eigenstate spatial distributions for each boundary condition: under PBC in both directions the eigenstates distribute uniformly across the 2D lattice (no localization); under PBC in $x$ and OBC in $y$ the eigenstates localize toward an open boundary (edge localization); under OBC in both $x$ and $y$ the eigenstates localize exponentially toward a single corner of the square lattice (the corner with large $j_x$ and $j_y$ indices). These distributions are obtained by averaging the spatial probability density over all eigenstates and plotting the resulting spatial map.
Fig. 2

Interpret these numerical observations as the two-dimensional non-Hermitian corner skin effect (NH corner skin effect): the exponential accumulation of eigenstates at the corner under OBC in both directions, with intermediate edge localization when only one direction is open, indicates a directional non-reciprocal bulk tendency that pushes bulk eigenstates toward boundaries and ultimately a corner when both directions have open boundaries.

Relate the NHSE to concomitant changes in the complex eigenspectrum when boundary conditions are varied: the computed spectra on the complex plane show notable boundary-condition-dependent features, with in-gap (line-gap) topological edge states becoming visible when open boundaries are present. Specifically, the spectrum and the presence of edge-state lines change between PBC and OBC, consistent with the non-Hermitian-sensitivity of bulk spectral topology.
Fig. 2

motivating_questions.content: Non-Hermitian skin effects in quantum systems had been observed experimentally in one-dimensional settings, where all eigenstates become exponentially localized toward a boundary under open boundary conditions, and the resulting directional bulk flow can be detected dynamically. For two spatial dimensions, higher-order skin phenomena (corner accumulation) had only been demonstrated in classical platforms, and it was unclear whether a realistic cold-atom Raman lattice with experimentally available laser-induced loss and Raman couplings could host a corner skin effect. Absent such a demonstration, one could not predict how eigenstate localization depends on boundary conditions in a 2D quantum Raman lattice, nor how spectral features on the complex plane evolve with boundary geometry; this prevented proposing experimentally accessible signatures of a 2D NHSE in cold-atom settings.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
Exact diagonalization (ED) of finite $\{10,5\}$ flakes (constructed via recursive Poincaré-disk epochs up to four epochs, 7040 sites) reveals: (i) for the Hermitian and non-Hermitian ($i\delta\sigma_z$) cases, the open-boundary spectrum is a subset of the hyperbolic band-theory (HBT) spectrum (ED $\subset$ HBT), consistent with a recent theorem; (ii) the cumulative density of states (measured against $\operatorname{Re}E$) computed from ED deviates from the k-space HBT density because (a) a macroscopic fraction of sites lie on the boundary and (b) automorphic Bloch theory omits states transforming in higher-dimensional irreps; (iii) adding non-reciprocal intra-unit-cell hopping ($\Omega$) produces enhanced localization of eigenstates concentrated at outer epochs (boundary localization whose magnitude and asymmetry increase with $\Omega$), measurable via the boundary inverse participation ratio
$$
\mathrm{IPR}_n=\frac{\sum_{r\in\text{boundary}}|\langle r|\psi_n\rangle|^2}{\sum_{r}|\langle r|\psi_n\rangle|^2},
$$
but this observed localization does not show the characteristic extensive spectral shift of a non-Hermitian skin effect in the models considered; instead it manifests as an enhanced boundary-weighted probability amplified by the preexisting macroscopic boundary fraction.

A two-band hyperbolic tight-binding Bloch Hamiltonian for the $\{10,5\}$ tessellation is written in the sublattice basis as
      $$
      \hat{H}_0(\mathbf{k})=\begin{pmatrix}
      M & -t\,h(\mathbf{k})\\[6pt]
      -t\,h(\mathbf{k})^{*} & -M
      \end{pmatrix},
      $$
      with the off-diagonal phase factor defined by
      $$
      h(\mathbf{k})\;=\;1+e^{ik_1}+e^{ik_2}+e^{ik_3}+e^{ik_4},
      $$
      where $\mathbf{k}=(k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4)$ are crystal momenta associated to four independent hyperbolic translation generators, $M$ is a sublattice potential (on-site energy difference) and $t$ the nearest-neighbour hopping amplitude (set to $t=1$ in illustrative results). Non-Hermiticity is introduced by adding $\;i\delta\sigma_z\;$ (balanced on-site gain and loss), $\;i\Omega\sigma_x\;$ or $\;i\Gamma\sigma_y\;$ (non-reciprocal intra-cell hopping) to $\hat{H}_0$. For these perturbations the band eigenvalues are given in closed form:
      $$
      E_{\pm}(\mathbf{k})=\pm\sqrt{|h(\mathbf{k})|^2-\delta^2}\quad(\text{for }i\delta\sigma_z),
      $$
      $$
      E_{\pm}(\mathbf{k})=\pm\sqrt{|h(\mathbf{k})|^2+M^2-\Omega^2+2i\Omega\operatorname{Re}h(\mathbf{k})}\quad(\text{for }i\Omega\sigma_x),
      $$
      $$
      E_{\pm}(\mathbf{k})=\pm\sqrt{|h(\mathbf{k})|^2+M^2-\Gamma^2-2i\Gamma\operatorname{Im}h(\mathbf{k})}\quad(\text{for }i\Gamma\sigma_y).
      $$
      These explicit forms define the criteria for gap closings and the complex spectral structure of non-Hermitian hyperbolic graphene.

Report the observed relationship between the two spectra: the OBC spectrum is a subset of the HBT spectrum (ED \( \subset \) HBT) for the Hermitian case and for the non-Hermitian case with  \( i\delta\sigma_z \) balanced gain/loss, consistent with the cited theorem that open-boundary spectra are contained in periodic-boundary spectra under the considered conditions.

Compare cumulative density-of-states (cumulative DOS) computed from k-space HBT and from ED with OBC while clarifying definitions: define the cumulative probability  \( p(E) \)  as the fraction of states with energy less than or equal to  \( E \)  when energies are ordered by their real parts (i.e., use  \( \operatorname{Re}E \)  as the axis for DOS comparison). Report the observed deviations between the HBT cumulative DOS and the ED cumulative DOS and attribute them to two causes explicitly noted by the authors: (a) the macroscopic fraction of sites that lie on the boundary in hyperbolic flakes, which biases OBC spectral statistics, and (b) omission by automorphic Bloch theory of eigenstates that transform in higher-dimensional irreducible representations of the non-Abelian translation group (automorphic Bloch theory only captures the U(1) automorphic sector). Introduce the boundary inverse participation ratio (boundary IPR) as a diagnostic of boundary localization for an eigenstate  \( |\psi_{n}\rangle \) : define the IPR of eigenstate  \( n \)  with respect to the set of boundary sites as
$
\mathrm{IPR}_n=\frac{\sum_{r\in\text{boundary}}|\langle r|\psi_n\rangle|^2}{\sum_{r}|\langle r|\psi_n\rangle|^2},
$
where  \( |\langle r|\psi_n\rangle|^2 \)  is the probability weight of eigenstate  \( n \)  at real-space site  \( r \) . Use this quantity to quantify the fraction of wave-function weight at outer epochs and to compare across non-Hermitian parameter values.

Report the numerical findings on localization and the (non-)existence of a conventional non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE): upon adding non-reciprocal intra-unit-cell hopping  \( \Omega \)  the authors observe enhanced localization of eigenstates concentrated at outer epochs (increasing  \( \Omega \)  increases the magnitude of boundary-weighted probability and increases asymmetry in the spatial profile owing to unit-cell-definition asymmetries). However, the authors note that this observed boundary localization does not exhibit the hallmark extensive spectral shift associated with the NHSE (i.e., a macroscopic spectral winding and accumulation of an extensive fraction of eigenstates strictly as a spectral reorganization), and so they interpret the effect as boundary-weight amplification layered on top of the preexisting macroscopic boundary fraction rather than as a true NHSE.

Prior state: automorphic hyperbolic Bloch theory offers bulk spectra but does not account for boundary-dominated finite flakes and omits higher-dimensional-irrep sectors. steps.reasoning:
A non-Hermitian Hamiltonian $H$ is defined to have a point gap at a reference point $E \in \mathbb{C}$ if and only if its complex spectrum does not cross $E$, i.e., $\det(H-E) \neq 0$.
[46,56]

For a one-dimensional non-Hermitian Bloch Hamiltonian $H(k)$ with $k \in [0,2\pi]$ and a finite number of bands, the winding number is defined as
$$
W(E) := \int_{0}^{2\pi} \frac{dk}{2\pi i} \frac{d}{dk} \log \det(H(k)-E),
$$
which is integer-valued because $\det(H(k)-E)$ can be complex. This point-gap topology is intrinsic to non-Hermitian systems; in one-dimensional Hermitian systems without symmetry, topological phases are absent.
[46,56]

The authors construct a Hermitian Hamiltonian $\tilde{H}$ from $H$ and the reference energy $E$ as
$$
\tilde{H}:=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & H-E \\ H^\dagger - E^* & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Under periodic boundary conditions, a point gap for $H(k)$ at $E$ implies a real energy gap for $\tilde{H}(k)$, and vice versa. Additionally, $\tilde{H}$ respects chiral symmetry $\Gamma \tilde{H} \Gamma^{-1} = -\tilde{H}$ with $\Gamma:=\sigma_z$.
[46,56]

By the conventional bulk-boundary correspondence for Hermitian Hamiltonians, $\tilde{H}$ with a semi-infinite boundary (only one boundary) possesses topologically protected zero modes localized at the boundary, analogous to the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. The topological invariant for these zero modes coincides with $W(E)$.
[61,62,63,93]

For $W(E) < 0$, the zero modes of $\tilde{H}$ are of the form $(0, |E\rangle)^T$ with negative chirality ($\Gamma = -1$). This implies that $|E\rangle$ is a right eigenstate of $H$ with eigenvalue $E$ ($H|E\rangle = E|E\rangle$) and is localized at the boundary. For $W(E) > 0$, the zero modes are $(|E\rangle, 0)^T$ with positive chirality, implying that $|E\rangle$ is a right eigenstate of $H^\dagger$, i.e., a left eigenstate of $H$ ($\langle E| H = \langle E| E$), also localized at the boundary.
[94]

The above reasoning holds for every complex $E$ with $W(E) \neq 0$. Therefore, in the semi-infinite system $H_{\mathrm{SIBC}}$ (with only one boundary), there exists an infinite number of boundary modes with eigenenergies $E$ for all such $E$.

The periodic spectrum $\sigma[H(k)]$ forms closed curves in the complex-energy plane. Theorem I states: The spectrum of $H_{\mathrm{SIBC}}$ consists of $\sigma[H(k)]$ together with all points $E$ in the interior of the area enclosed by $\sigma[H(k)]$ for which $W(E) \neq 0$. For such $E$ with $W(E) < 0$ ($W(E) > 0$), $|E\rangle$ is a right (left) eigenstate of $H_{\mathrm{SIBC}}$ localized at the boundary. This is illustrated in Fig. 1(a), where the semi-infinite system shows boundary modes filling the interior of the periodic spectrum.
Fig. 1

motivating_questions.content: The winding number $W(E)$ was known as a topological invariant for point gaps [46,56], but its bulk-boundary correspondence was not established. In particular, for semi-infinite systems with only one boundary, it was unclear whether a nonzero winding number guarantees the existence of boundary modes at energy $E$. Without this understanding, the connection between point-gap topology and the skin effect in finite systems remained opaque, hindering the development of a unified BBC for non-Hermitian systems.

steps.reasoning: Define the one-dimensional staggered-hopping tight-binding lattice and all symbols: let $a_{n}^{\dagger}$ and $a_{n}$ denote the creation and annihilation operators on lattice site $n$; let $t_{n}$ denote the hopping (coupling) coefficient between sites $n$ and $n+1$ with $t_{n}=t_{1}$ for odd $n$ and $t_{n}=t_{2}$ for even $n$; define $t_{1}=1-\lambda\cos\Phi$ and $t_{2}=1+\lambda\cos\Phi$ with real parameter $\lambda$ satisfying $\lambda<1$, define the drive angular frequency $\omega$, and define the non-Hermitian amplitude $\gamma$ which parametrizes alternating gain ($\gamma>0$) and loss ($\gamma<0$) on lattice sites.

State the time- (propagation-) dependent Hamiltonian used for the driven system: the Hamiltonian as a function of propagation coordinate $z$ is
$H(z)=-\sum_{n}t_{n}a_{n}^{\dagger}a_{n+1}+{\rm h.c.}+\left(-1\right)^{n}i\gamma\cos(\omega z)a_{n}^{\dagger}a_{n},$
where ${\rm h.c.}$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate, and the on-site non-Hermitian term is the staggered periodically modulated potential $(-1)^{n}i\gamma\cos(\omega z)$.

Introduce Floquet theory and the Floquet Hamiltonian definitions used as the analytical framework: for a Hamiltonian periodic in $z$ with period $T=2\pi/\omega$ (i.e. $H(z)=H(z+T)$) there exist Floquet solutions of the form $\psi_{\alpha}(z)=e^{-i\epsilon_{\alpha}z}\Phi_{\alpha}(z)$ where $\Phi_{\alpha}(z)$ is $T$-periodic in $z$ and the time-independent quantities $\epsilon_{\alpha}$ are the Floquet quasi energies; define the Floquet Hamiltonian operator $H_{F}=H-i\partial/\partial z$ which satisfies $H_{F}\Phi_{\alpha}=\epsilon_{\alpha}\Phi_{\alpha}$ and note that Floquet quasi energies are $2\pi/T$-periodic in quasi energy. 
[27]

Write the momentum-space two-band form of the Hamiltonian under periodic boundary conditions and define symbols appearing there: assuming translational invariance (periodic boundary conditions) and defining the lattice spacing $a$ and crystal momentum $k$ with $-\pi/a<k<\pi/a$, the Hamiltonian matrix in the sublattice (two-component) basis is
$H(k,z)=t_{2}\sin(2ka)\,\sigma_{y}-\big(t_{1}+t_{2}\cos(2ka)\big)\,\sigma_{x}+i\gamma\cos(\omega z)\,\sigma_{z},$
where $\vec{\sigma}=(\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z})$ are the Pauli matrices.

Analyze the static ($\omega=0$) limit and define its band energies explicitly: set $\omega=0$ so that the on-site term reduces to $i\gamma\,\sigma_{z}$ (time-independent) and compute the two-band energy eigenvalues as
$E=\mp\sqrt{t_{1}^{2}+t_{2}^{2}+2t_{1}t_{2}\cos(2ka)-\gamma^{2}},$
where the upper/lower signs give the conduction and valence bands respectively. From this expression observe that the term $-\gamma^{2}$ can render the square-root argument negative at parameter values where the band gap closes in the Hermitian case, causing complex energy eigenvalues to appear in the non-Hermitian static model.

Use the static-band expression to show instability of topological transition in the non-driven case: set $t_{1}=t_{2}$ and $ka=\pi/2$ (the band-closing condition in the Hermitian SSH model) in the static energy expression to obtain a vanishing real-part argument of the square root and thereby note that nonzero $\gamma$ generically produces complex energies at the would-be transition; conclude that in the static ($\omega=0$) non-Hermitian model topological states are not stable because complex eigenvalues appear when the phase transition occurs.

State the numerical Floquet computation method used to obtain quasi-energy spectra for $\omega\neq 0$: construct a truncated Floquet Hamiltonian (matrix) by expanding Floquet states in Fourier harmonics indexed by integer $n$, and for numerical convergence use a truncation parameter $N_{F}$ large enough; the truncated Floquet Hamiltonian matrix used in computations has dimension $2(2N_{F}+1)\times 2(2N_{F}+1)$ (factor $2$ for the two-band internal space and $2N_{F}+1$ for harmonic indices). 
[29]

Report the central numerical observation for periodically driven ($\omega\neq 0$) case: numerically find that for sufficiently large drive frequency $\omega$ and for non-Hermitian amplitude $\gamma$ below a model-dependent critical value, the Floquet quasi-energy spectrum is entirely real (i.e. no complex quasi energies appear) and the system exhibits gapped quasi-energy bands that can close and reopen as coupling parameters are varied without inducing complex quasi energies.

Provide the specific numerical example parameters and describe the computed quasi-energy band behavior used to demonstrate the phase structure: for drive frequency $\omega=2\pi$, non-Hermitian amplitude $\gamma=1$, stagger parameter $\lambda=0.4$ (so that $t_{1}=1-0.4\cos\Phi$, $t_{2}=1+0.4\cos\Phi$), and crystal momentum $k$ plotting, the computed quasi-energy spectrum (periodic in quasi energy with period $\omega$ and periodic in $k$ with period $2\pi/a$) shows conduction and valence quasi-energy bands separated by a gap when $t_{2}<t_{1}$, a gap closing at $t_{2}=t_{1}$ occurring at $ka=\mp\pi/2$, and a reopening of the gap when $t_{2}>t_{1}$; the quasi-energy spectrum remains real throughout this continuous deformation. 
Fig. 1

Explain the topological distinction deduced from the gap-closing and reopening in the Floquet quasi-energy bands: define two periodically driven systems to be topologically equivalent if their quasi-energy band structures can be smoothly deformed into each other without closing the quasi-energy gap while respecting the Hamiltonian symmetries; since the deformation from $t_{2}<t_{1}$ to $t_{2}>t_{1}$ necessarily closes the gap at $t_{2}=t_{1}$, the two regimes are topologically distinct; identify the regime $t_{1}>t_{2}$ as topologically trivial and the regime $t_{1}<t_{2}$ as topologically nontrivial (supporting protected edge states) in the driven model.

Describe numerical results under open boundary conditions that demonstrate the presence of topologically protected edge states in the nontrivial driven regime: adopt open boundary conditions on a finite lattice with $N$ sites (edge sites at $n=1$ and $n=N$) and compute the Floquet quasi-energy spectrum for $N=40$ with parameters $\gamma=1$, $\lambda=0.4$, and $\omega=2\pi$ as a function of the phase parameter $\Phi$; the computed spectrum shows states appearing within the quasi-energy bulk gap for parameter ranges where $t_{1}<t_{2}$ (specifically when $\Phi$ lies outside $(\pi/2,3\pi/2)$ the system is nontrivial), demonstrating topologically protected edge states in the driven non-Hermitian model. 
Fig. 1

Report the computed behavior of edge-state dynamics and their distinction between topologically trivial and nontrivial driven cases: construct an initial edge-state obtained in the Hermitian limit ($\gamma=0$) and propagate it in the driven non-Hermitian system with $\gamma=1$ and $\omega=2\pi$; for the nontrivial parameter choice $\Phi=0$ (which gives $t_{1}=0.4$, $t_{2}=1.6$) the edge state remains localized (protected) while for the trivial choice $\Phi=\pi/2$ (which gives $t_{1}=1.4$, $t_{2}=0.4$) the edge excitation delocalizes; additionally, in the driven non-Hermitian case the edge-state density oscillates during propagation rather than growing without bound, and this oscillation is attributed to the real quasi-energy spectrum of the driven Hamiltonian. 
Fig. 2

State the numerically observed critical non-Hermitian strength at which the driven Floquet quasi-energy spectrum develops complex eigenvalues and topological stability is lost: fixing the drive frequency at $\omega=2\pi$, numerical computations indicate a critical non-Hermitian amplitude $\gamma_{c}\approx 3.6$ above which complex quasi-energy eigenvalues appear and the driven system becomes topologically unstable (the real part of the spectrum changes dramatically once complex quasi energies appear).

Conclude from the above arguments and numerical evidence that the periodically driven one-dimensional staggered-hopping (SSH-type) non-Hermitian lattice with periodically modulated staggered on-site potential $(-1)^{n}i\gamma\cos(\omega z)$ supports stable Floquet topological phases: when the drive frequency $\omega$ is sufficiently large and the non-Hermitian amplitude $\gamma$ is below a model-dependent critical value (numerically $\gamma_{c}\approx 3.6$ at $\omega=2\pi$), the Floquet quasi-energy spectrum can be entirely real, the quasi-energy bands undergo a gap-closing at $t_{1}=t_{2}$ and reopen without complex quasi energies, the regimes $t_{1}<t_{2}$ and $t_{1}>t_{2}$ are topologically distinct, and topologically protected edge states appear under open boundary conditions (numerical examples used $\omega=2\pi$, $\lambda=0.4$, $N=40$, and $\gamma=1$ to display gapped quasi-energy bands and edge states).

motivating_questions.content: In one-dimensional bipartite tight-binding lattices (the SSH class) with staggered hopping amplitudes, topological phases are identified by band-gap closings as a control parameter is varied (here parameterized by $\Phi$ giving $t_{1}=1-\lambda\cos\Phi$, $t_{2}=1+\lambda\cos\Phi$). Prior to this work, adding static PT-symmetric non-Hermitian on-site terms ($i\gamma$ alternating sign on sublattices) made the energy eigenvalues generically complex at or near the band-gap closing points, so the usual indicators of topological phase transitions and protected edge modes became ill-defined because the spectrum lost reality at the transition. Consequently, one could not claim a stable topological insulator phase in such non-driven non-Hermitian SSH models: the instability (complex energies) prevented a robust bulk gap and protected edge states. The scientific need is therefore to determine whether time-periodic (Floquet) modulation of the PT-symmetric non-Hermitian term can preserve spectral reality through the transition and thereby recover a well-defined topological distinction and robust localized edge modes in a concrete 1D lattice setting.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A modified periodic boundary condition (mpbc) \(\psi(x+L) = b^L \psi(x)\) with a real positive constant \(b\) is introduced to define a bulk geometry for non-Hermitian lattice systems. In this framework, eigenstates take the generalized Bloch form \(\psi(x) = \beta^x u(x)\) with \(\beta = b e^{i k}\), and the allowed \(\beta\) values lie on a circle of radius \(b\) in the complex plane, forming a generalized Brillouin zone. The boundary Hamiltonian that realizes this mpbc for a tight-binding model is given by adding hopping terms between the first and last sites multiplied by factors \(b^{-L}\) (forward hopping) and \(b^{L}\) (backward hopping). For the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model with intra-cell and inter-cell non-reciprocal hoppings, the total Hamiltonian under mpbc reads \(H_{\mathrm{mpbc}}^{\mathrm{SSH}}(b) = H_{\mathrm{SSH}}^{(L)} + H_{bd}^{\mathrm{SSH}}(b)\) where \(H_{bd}^{\mathrm{SSH}}(b)\) contains the boundary terms \(b^{-L}t_2^+|1,A\rangle\langle L,B| + b^{L}t_2^-|L,B\rangle\langle 1,A|\) and analogous third-nearest-neighbor contributions. The eigenvalue problem reduces to a \(2\times 2\) generalized Bloch Hamiltonian \(H_{\mathrm{mpbc}}(\beta)\) with off-diagonal entries \(R_+(\beta)=t_1^+ + t_2^-\beta + t_3\beta^{-1}\) and \(R_-(\beta)=t_1^- + t_2^+\beta^{-1} + t_3\beta\), and the energy spectrum is determined by \(R_+(\beta)R_-(\beta) = E^2\).

conclusion.content:
A modified periodic boundary condition (mpbc) for a one-dimensional lattice of length L is defined by the relation ψ(x+L) = b^L ψ(x) with b a real positive constant and ψ(x) the lattice-site amplitude at site x; under this mpbc the eigenstates take the generalized Bloch form ψ(x)=β^x u(x) with β = b e^{ik} and u(x) a cell-periodic spinor, so that the allowed β values lie on the circle |β|=b in the complex β-plane and thus define a generalized Brillouin zone. For a tight-binding realization of the mpbc one adds boundary hopping terms that couple the last unit cell x=L back to the first unit cell x=1 with amplitude factors b^{-L} multiplying the forward-hopping matrix elements and b^{L} multiplying the backward-hopping matrix elements; in the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model with two sublattices A,B and with intra-cell hoppings t_1^± = t_1 ± γ_1, inter-cell hoppings t_2^± = t_2 ± γ_2, and third-nearest-neighbor hopping t_3, the boundary Hamiltonian concretizing the mpbc is
      H_bd^{SSH}(b) = b^{-L} t_2^+ |1,A⟩⟨L,B| + b^{L} t_2^- |L,B⟩⟨1,A| + b^{-L} t_3 |1,B⟩⟨L,A| + b^{L} t_3 |L,A⟩⟨1,B|,
      and the total mpbc Hamiltonian is H_mpbc^{SSH}(b)=H_{SSH}^{(L)}+H_bd^{SSH}(b). Diagonalizing H_mpbc^{SSH}(b) with the Ansatz |β⟩ = Σ_{x=1}^L β^x (u_A|x,A⟩+u_B|x,B⟩) (with β^L=b^L) reduces the eigenvalue problem to a 2×2 generalized Bloch Hamiltonian
      H_mpbc(β) = [[0, R_-(β)],[R_+(β), 0]],
      where R_+(β)=t_1^+ + t_2^- β + t_3 β^{-1} and R_-(β)=t_1^- + t_2^+ β^{-1} + t_3 β, and the complex energy E(β) satisfies the secular equation R_+(β) R_-(β) = E^2.

steps.reasoning: For a one-dimensional lattice system with translational symmetry, generalized Bloch eigenstates are taken to satisfy $\psi(x+1)=\beta \psi(x)$, so the wave function has the form $\psi(x)=\beta^x u(x)$, where $u(x)$ is periodic with period one and $\beta$ is the lattice translation eigenvalue.

In a Hermitian infinite crystal, boundedness of the wave function forces $|\beta|=1$, which reduces the generalized Bloch form to the usual plane-wave form $\psi(x)=e^{ikx}u(x)$ with $\beta=e^{ik}$ and $k \in [0,2\pi]$. By contrast, in non-Hermitian systems the physically relevant bulk states under open boundary conditions can have $|\beta|\neq 1$, so the standard periodic boundary condition $\psi(x+L)=\psi(x)$ is too restrictive because it only permits $|\beta|=1$.

To define a bulk geometry that admits the natural amplitude variation of non-Hermitian bulk states, the boundary condition is modified to $\psi(x+L)=b^L \psi(x)$, where $b$ is a real positive constant. This modified periodic boundary condition selects generalized Bloch states satisfying $\beta^L=b^L$, hence $\beta=be^{ik}$ with $k=2\pi n/L$, and the allowed $\beta$ values lie on a circle of radius $b$ in the complex $\beta$-plane.

For a tight-binding chain, this modified periodic boundary condition is implemented by closing the chain with boundary hopping terms multiplied by factors $b^{-L}$ for hopping from the last site to the first and $b^L$ for hopping from the first site to the last, so that the boundary Hamiltonian realizes the chosen amplitude factor in the wave function.

For the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with intra-cell and inter-cell non-reciprocal hoppings $t_1^\pm=t_1\pm \gamma_1$ and $t_2^\pm=t_2\pm \gamma_2$, together with third-nearest-neighbor hopping $t_3$, the total Hamiltonian under the modified periodic boundary condition is the sum of the finite-chain bulk Hamiltonian and the boundary coupling terms. The boundary terms connect the final unit cell back to the first one with amplitudes $b^{-L}t_2^+$, $b^Lt_2^-$, $b^{-L}t_3$, and $b^Lt_3$ in the appropriate matrix elements.

With the generalized Bloch ansatz $|\beta\rangle=\sum_{x=1}^{L}\beta^x(u_A|x,A\rangle+u_B|x,B\rangle)$ and $\beta=be^{ik}$, the eigenvalue problem reduces to a $2\times 2$ generalized Bloch Hamiltonian of chiral form,
        \[
        H_{mpbc}(\beta)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & R_-(\beta) \\ R_+(\beta) & 0\end{bmatrix},
        \]
        where
        \[
        R_+(\beta)=t_1^+ + t_2^- \beta + t_3 \beta^{-1}, \qquad R_-(\beta)=t_1^- + t_2^+ \beta^{-1} + t_3 \beta.
        \]
        The secular equation is therefore $R_+(\beta)R_-(\beta)=E^2$.

Thus the modified periodic boundary condition defines a non-Hermitian bulk geometry through a generalized Brillouin zone given by the circle $|\beta|=b$, and in this geometry the spectrum is determined by the generalized Bloch Hamiltonian rather than by the standard $|\beta|=1$ Bloch theory.

motivating_questions.content: In the study of topological phases, it is essential to have a clean separation between bulk and boundary properties, which in Hermitian systems is provided by the periodic boundary condition. For non-Hermitian topological insulators, the standard pbc selects only \(\beta = e^{i k}\) (\(|\beta|=1\)) from the generalized Bloch solutions \(\beta^x u(x)\). This restriction fails to account for the natural amplitude variation (non-Hermitian skin effect) that characterizes the true bulk states under open boundaries, causing the pbc spectrum to differ qualitatively from the obc spectrum and breaking the bulk-boundary correspondence. There was no known boundary condition that could, like the pbc in the Hermitian case, yield a bulk geometry whose spectrum and topological invariants are directly tied to the existence of edge states.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: Computing the non-Bloch topological invariant $W$ on the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ) for the corresponding non-Bloch Hamiltonian $H_\beta$ yields a topologically nontrivial region where $W=1$. For the parameters $r=0.5$, $\gamma=1$ the numerically obtained non-Bloch winding number takes $W=1$ for intracell hopping values $v\in[-0.559,\,0.559]$ (with $W=0$ outside this interval). The non-Bloch invariant correctly predicts the appearance and edge-localization of the near-zero open-boundary modes and corresponds to the parameter window in which the numerical dynamics exhibit edge-dominated decay probability imbalance. By contrast, the conventional Bloch winding number computed from the Bloch Hamiltonian does not align with the finite-chain edge-mode regime (it attains fractional $1/2$ values and fails to predict the open-boundary modes), showing the necessity of the non-Bloch invariant for bulk-boundary correspondence in this lossy model.

The system is formulated by a non-Hermitian tight-binding Hamiltonian with pure loss on sublattice B and Hermitian intracell and intercell hoppings. In real space, the Hamiltonian is
      $$
      H=\sum_{m}\Big[-\frac{i\gamma}{2}\hat{c}_{m,B}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m,B}+\nu\big(\hat{c}_{m,A}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m,B}+\hat{c}_{m,B}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m,A}\big)
      +\frac{i\gamma}{2}\big(\hat{c}_{m+1,A}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m,A}-\hat{c}_{m,A}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m+1,A}\big)
      -\frac{i\gamma}{2}\big(\hat{c}_{m+1,B}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m,B}-\hat{c}_{m,B}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m+1,B}\big)
      +\frac{\gamma}{2}\big(\hat{c}_{m+1,A}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m,B}+\hat{c}_{m,B}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m+1,A}\big)
      +\frac{\gamma}{2}\big(\hat{c}_{m+1,B}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m,A}+\hat{c}_{m,A}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{m+1,B}\big)\Big],
      $$
      where $\hat c_{m,A}^{\dagger}$ and $\hat c_{m,B}^{\dagger}$ create a particle on site A and B of unit cell $m$, the loss (decay) rate on each B site is $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$, and the intracell (A–B) hopping is $v$ (real). In the momentum-space representation, the Bloch Hamiltonian is $H_k = (v + r\cos k)\sigma_x + (r\sin k + i\gamma/4)\sigma_z - i\gamma/4 I$, where $r$ is the intercell hopping strength (real, set to $r=0.5$ in numerical work). The single-particle continuous-time dynamics for amplitudes $\psi_m^A(t)=\langle mA|\psi(t)\rangle$ and $\psi_m^B(t)=\langle mB|\psi(t)\rangle$ follow from $i\dot\psi = H\psi$ and satisfy the norm-decay relation
      $$
      \frac{d}{dt}\langle\psi|\psi\rangle = -\sum_m\gamma\,|\psi_m^B(t)|^2.
      $$
      For an initial state localized on an A site $o$ with $\psi_m^A(0)=\delta_{mo},\ \psi_m^B(0)=0$, the final spatial distribution of decay events is defined and computable as
      $$
      P_m = \int_0^\infty\gamma\,|\psi_m^B(t)|^2\,dt,\qquad \sum_m P_m=1.
      $$
      This provides a concrete, operational mapping from the microscopic non-Hermitian lattice Hamiltonian and its continuous-time propagation to the measurable decay-position probabilities $P_m$.

steps.reasoning: Start from the established lattice model and single-particle dynamics (conclusion 1): the non-Hermitian tight-binding Hamiltonian with parameters $v$, $r$, and $ \gamma $ and the single-particle equations of motion for amplitudes $ \psi_{m}^{A,B}(t) $; use these to construct momentum-space Hamiltonians and to analyze topological invariants.

Pass to momentum (Bloch) space by a Fourier transform; define crystal momentum $k$ and write the Bloch Hamiltonian as
$$
H_{k}=h_{x}\,\sigma_{x}+\Big(h_{z}+\frac{i\gamma}{4}\Big)\sigma_{z}-\frac{i\gamma}{4}I,
$$
where $h_{x}=v+r\cos k$, $h_{z}=r\sin k$, $I$ is the $2\times 2$ identity matrix, and $\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z}$ are the Pauli matrices; an overall constant non-Hermitian shift $-\frac{i\gamma}{4}I$ can be separated and removed for topological considerations to define $H_{k}^{\prime}=h_{x}\sigma_{x}+(h_{z}+i\gamma/4)\sigma_{z}$.

Note that the conventional Bloch winding number computed from $H_{k}^{\prime}$ as $k$ traverses the Brillouin zone is numerically found not to match the open-boundary edge-mode regime: the Bloch winding number attains fractional values $1/2$ in certain parameter regions and fails to predict the edge modes observed in finite open chains, motivating the use of a non-Bloch formulation that replaces $e^{ik}$ by generalized complex parameters on a generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ). 
Fig. 7

Perform a unitary rotation about the $x$ axis via $e^{i\pi\sigma_{x}/4}$ which maps $\sigma_{x}\to\sigma_{x}$ and $\sigma_{z}\to\sigma_{y}$, thereby transforming $H_{k}^{\prime}$ into a form convenient for non-Bloch replacement; denote the rotated Hamiltonian symbolically and then implement the non-Bloch substitution $e^{ik}\to\beta$ and $e^{-ik}\to\beta^{-1}$ where $ \beta $ is a complex parameter defined on the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ).
[77, 78]

Write the resulting non-Bloch Hamiltonian $H_{\beta}$ explicitly in terms of raising and lowering Pauli operators $ \sigma_{\pm}=(\sigma_{x}\pm i\sigma_{y})/2 $ as
$$
H_{\beta}=\left(v+\frac{\gamma}{4}+r\beta^{-1}\right)\sigma_{+}+\left(v-\frac{\gamma}{4}+r\beta\right)\sigma_{-},
$$
where $ \beta $ parametrizes the GBZ contour that replaces the Bloch phase factor $e^{ik}$ in the non-Hermitian band theory.

Define right and left eigenvectors of $H_{\beta}$ as $|u_{R}(\beta)\rangle$ and $\langle u_{L}(\beta)|$, and introduce $|\tilde{u}_{R}(\beta)\rangle\equiv\sigma_{z}|u_{R}(\beta)\rangle$ and $|\tilde{u}_{L}(\beta)\rangle\equiv\sigma_{z}|u_{L}(\beta)\rangle$; using these, construct the generalized $Q$ matrix as
$$
Q(\beta)=|\tilde{u}_{R}(\beta)\rangle\langle\tilde{u}_{L}(\beta)|-|u_{R}(\beta)\rangle\langle u_{L}(\beta)|,
$$
which is off-diagonal and can be represented in the form $\begin{pmatrix}q & -1\\ q^{-1} & -q\end{pmatrix}$ up to conventions for the off-diagonal scalar function $q(\beta)$.
[87]

Define the non-Bloch winding number $W$ on the GBZ by integrating $q^{-1}dq$ around the GBZ contour:
$$
W=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_{GBZ} q^{-1}\,dq,
$$
so $W$ counts how $q(\beta)$ winds as $\beta$ traverses the GBZ and serves as the non-Bloch topological invariant appropriate for predicting open-boundary edge modes in non-Hermitian systems.

Numerically compute $W$ for the parameter choice $r=0.5$ and $ \gamma=1 $ as a function of the intracell hopping $v$ by evaluating the $q(\beta)$ integral on the numerically determined GBZ; the result is that $W=1$ for intracell hopping values $v\in[-0.559,\,0.559]$ and $W=0$ outside this interval.
Fig. 7

Compare the non-Bloch invariant $W$ with the open-boundary spectral data: the parameter window where $W=1$ coincides with the parameter range in which near-zero open-boundary modes (edge modes) appear in the finite-chain spectrum and are localized at physical edges; because the Bloch winding number (computed from the Bloch Hamiltonian) does not align with this finite-chain edge-mode regime and even takes fractional $1/2$ values, the non-Bloch invariant is necessary for establishing bulk-boundary correspondence in this lossy model.

motivating_questions.content: Standard Bloch-based topological invariants computed in momentum space do not reliably predict edge-localized states of finite non-Hermitian open chains; consequently one cannot use Bloch invariants to forecast the parameter regimes where spectral edge modes (and the associated anomalous dynamical decay) will occur. A predictive topological diagnostic is required that (i) is defined for non-Hermitian models, (ii) accounts for non-Bloch boundary-sensitive eigenmode deformation (GBZ), and (iii) correlates with both spectral edge modes and dynamical signatures such as $P_m$. Without the non-Bloch invariant one lacks a quantitative map from microscopic parameters $(v,r,\gamma)$ to the existence of edge modes and to the observed edge-concentrated decay.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: When the bulk and boundary of a closed Hermitian system are conceptually treated as an environment and a system, respectively, the effective boundary Hamiltonian becomes non-Hermitian and acquires nontrivial topology. For a Hermitian Hamiltonian H with bulk part H_bulk, edge part H_edge, and coupling T, projecting out the bulk yields the effective non-Hermitian edge Hamiltonian H_eff(E) = H_edge + Σ(E), where the self-energy Σ(E) = T^† (E + iη − H_bulk)^(−1) T captures the continuous exchange of particles between bulk and boundary. The non-Hermiticity of Σ(E) emerges from the finite lifetimes of quasiparticles that escape from the boundary into the bulk, and this self-energy bridges Hermitian bulk topology and non-Hermitian boundary topology: it detects the former and induces the latter.

steps.reasoning: Start from the closed Hermitian system written as a block Hamiltonian $H=\begin{pmatrix}H_{\mathrm{bulk}} & T\\ T^{\dagger} & H_{\mathrm{edge}}\end{pmatrix}$, where $H_{\mathrm{bulk}}$ is the bulk Hamiltonian, $H_{\mathrm{edge}}$ is the boundary Hamiltonian, and $T$ is the bulk-boundary coupling. The bulk is conceptually treated as an environment and the boundary as the system.

Introduce the retarded Green's function $G$ by $[(E+\mathrm{i}\eta)-H]G=1$, where $E$ is the energy and $\eta>0$ is an infinitesimal quantity enforcing causality. Writing this in block form and eliminating the bulk amplitudes yields an effective boundary equation of the form $(E+\mathrm{i}\eta-H_{\mathrm{edge}}-\Sigma)G_{\mathrm{edge}}=1$.

The self-energy is therefore $\Sigma(E)=T^{\dagger}(E+\mathrm{i}\eta-H_{\mathrm{bulk}})^{-1}T$. The effective boundary Hamiltonian is $H_{\mathrm{eff}}(E)=H_{\mathrm{edge}}+\Sigma(E)$. This expresses the boundary dynamics after the bulk degrees of freedom are projected out.

The self-energy $\Sigma(E)$ represents continuous particle exchange between boundary and bulk through the coupling $T$. Because the bulk can absorb amplitude from the boundary, the boundary quasiparticles acquire finite lifetimes; this is the origin of the non-Hermiticity of $\Sigma(E)$.

The same self-energy also carries the topological information of the bulk into the boundary theory. The paper states that the self-energy detects Hermitian bulk topology and induces non-Hermitian boundary topology, so the effective boundary Hamiltonian becomes the bridge between closed-system topology and open-system topology.

Equivalently, by viewing the bulk and boundary as environment and system, respectively, the boundary Hamiltonian becomes non-Hermitian even though the full Hamiltonian $H$ is Hermitian. This establishes the claimed effective non-Hermitian boundary Hamiltonian and its topological content.

motivating_questions.content: Hermitian topological insulators exhibit the celebrated bulk-boundary correspondence, where nontrivial bulk topology guarantees the existence of anomalous gapless boundary states. Meanwhile, non-Hermitian systems—where the Hamiltonian is not equal to its Hermitian conjugate—exhibit a fundamentally different kind of topology characterized by point gaps in complex energy spectra, giving rise to phenomena such as the non-Hermitian skin effect, where vast numbers of eigenstates collapse to boundaries. Although topological classification had formally suggested a correspondence between Hermitian topology in d dimensions and non-Hermitian topology in d−1 dimensions, all prior realizations required non-Hermiticity to be added as an external perturbation, such as gain or loss introduced into photonic or phononic lattices. There was no established mechanism for non-Hermitian topology to arise intrinsically from a purely Hermitian system. The fundamental obstacle was the lack of a conceptual framework that could partition a closed Hermitian system into subsystems in such a way that the subsystem dynamics naturally acquire non-Hermiticity with topological content inherited from the original Hermitian topology.

First, the time-averaged center-of-mass M̄_μ (averaged over T=600 ħ/J) computed from open-boundary wave-packet dynamics shows a nonzero value with the same sign on both legs when g_b ≠ -g_a, indicating population accumulation at one boundary. Second, the spectral winding number w computed from the periodic-boundary Bloch Hamiltonian is nonzero (w=2) for the same parameter region (g_b ≠ -g_a) and zero only at g_b = -g_a. The agreement between these two independent approaches—one dynamical and one spectral—strongly supports the identification of the antichiral dynamical behavior (same-direction currents on both legs) with the NHSE-induced skin accumulation on both legs.

The spectral winding provides a topological basis that is robust to simulation details (time step, normalization procedure, initial state choice). This directly underwrites the mechanism/attribution layer of the conclusion\u2014antichiral dynamics is indeed the NHSE in this system."}

Define the spectral winding number $w$ used to detect the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE): for each band $n\in\{1,2\}$ choose a base energy $E_B^{(n)}$ lying inside the loop traced by $E_n(k)$ in the complex-energy plane, and define
$ w=\sum_{n=1}^2\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{\partial_k}{2\pi}\arg\big[E_n(k)-E_B^{(n)}\big].$
Here $\arg(\cdot)$ denotes the complex argument (phase) of its argument; the derivative $\partial_k$ integrates the phase winding of the band energy around the chosen base point as $k$ traverses the Brillouin zone. The winding number is an integer that characterizes enclosed loops of the complex band energies.

Explain the bulk-edge correspondence linking nonzero winding $w$ to NHSE under open boundaries: if a chosen base energy $E_B$ lies inside a closed complex-energy loop described by a band under periodic boundary conditions, then a nonzero winding number $w$ indicates the presence of $|w|$ localized edge modes at energy $E=E_B$ under open boundary conditions; the sign of $w$ determines whether these modes localize at the left or right boundary. The authors attribute this correspondence to the cited theoretical framework on spectral topology for non-Hermitian systems.

motivating_questions.content: The NHSE is known to relate to spectral winding under periodic boundary conditions, but magnetic fields can suppress or alter skin phenomena in higher-dimensional lattices. For a two-leg ladder with synthetic flux and nonreciprocal hoppings, it was not established whether a nonzero spectral winding (hence NHSE) appears, how it depends on the nonreciprocity parameters $g_{a,b}$ and flux $\phi$, and whether a nonzero winding gives rise to antichiral dynamics (same-direction currents on both legs) under open boundaries. Thus, the relation between bulk topological invariants computed with periodic boundary conditions and the number and nature of edge states in finite samples is fundamentally altered in the presence of non-Hermiticity and defectiveness.

An explicit non-Hermitian tight-binding model is realized by classical complex amplitudes $\alpha_n,\beta_n$ on two sublattices per unit cell whose linear equations of motion are
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      \dot{\alpha}_{n}=& \tfrac{\gamma}{2} \alpha_{n}-i v \beta_{n}+\tfrac{r}{2}\left(\alpha_{n-1}-\alpha_{n+1}\right)-\tfrac{i r}{2}\left(\beta_{n-1}+\beta_{n+1}\right), \\
      \dot{\beta}_{n}=&-\tfrac{\gamma}{2} \beta_{n}-i v \alpha_{n}-\tfrac{r}{2}\left(\beta_{n-1}-\beta_{n+1}\right)-\tfrac{i r}{2}\left(\alpha_{n-1}+\alpha_{n+1}\right),
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      for $n=1,\dots,N$. These equations are equivalent to unitary-time evolution (Schrödinger-like) under a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian $H$ whose momentum-space Bloch Hamiltonian is $H_k = h_x(k)\sigma_x + (h_z(k)+i\gamma/2)\sigma_z$ with $h_x(k)=v+r\cos k$ and $h_z(k)=r\sin k$. Parameters: $\gamma$ is sublattice gain (on $\alpha$) and loss (on $\beta$), $v$ and $r$ are Hermitian hopping amplitudes. The model explicitly breaks Hermiticity while preserving a chiral symmetry $\Gamma H\Gamma=-H$ with $\Gamma=\bigoplus_n\sigma_{y,n}$ and having $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry with $\mathcal{P}=\bigoplus_n\sigma_{x,n}$ and time reversal $\mathcal{T}$.

For an open finite chain of $N$ unit cells (total $2N$ sites) of the non-Hermitian tight-binding model with sublattice gain/loss $\gamma$, Hermitian hopping amplitudes $v$ and $r$, and long-range hopping, the equations of motion are
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      \dot{\alpha}_{n}=& \tfrac{\gamma}{2} \alpha_{n}-i v \beta_{n}+\tfrac{r}{2}\left(\alpha_{n-1}-\alpha_{n+1}\right)-\tfrac{i r}{2}\left(\beta_{n-1}+\beta_{n+1}\right), \\
      \dot{\beta}_{n}=&-\tfrac{\gamma}{2} \beta_{n}-i v \alpha_{n}-\tfrac{r}{2}\left(\beta_{n-1}-\beta_{n+1}\right)-\tfrac{i r}{2}\left(\alpha_{n-1}+\alpha_{n+1}\right),
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      for $n=1,\dots,N$. The Hamiltonian $H$ shows, in parameter regimes where a real-part band gap opens near $v=\gamma/2$, an eigenvalue at $E=0$ that is algebraically twofold degenerate but has geometric multiplicity one (i.e., it is defective). The associated eigenvector $u_0$ is exponentially localized on a single edge (left edge for $v>0$, right edge for $v<0$), and there exists a generalized eigenvector $u_0'$ satisfying $H u_0' = u_0$. The defective zero-energy eigenvalue appears inside the open-chain band gap and disappears (splits into the bands) when that gap closes.

The momentum-space $2\times 2$ non-Hermitian Hamiltonian
      $$
      H_k = h_x(k)\sigma_x + \bigl(h_z(k)+\tfrac{i\gamma}{2}\bigr)\sigma_z,
      $$
      with $h_x(k)=v+r\cos k$ and $h_z(k)=r\sin k$, has eigenvectors that are $4\pi$ periodic in $k$ when the closed trajectory $(h_x(k),h_z(k))$ encircles a single exceptional point, so that the usual $2\pi$ sweep of $k$ does not return an eigenvector to itself. The topological winding number defined by the trajectory of $(\langle\sigma_x\rangle,\langle\sigma_z\rangle)$ for a single eigenvector thus takes the fractional value $1/2$ (one half) when $H_k$ encircles exactly one exceptional point; it is $0$ when no exceptional point is encircled and $1$ when two are encircled. The winding number here is computed by following an eigenvector through the Brillouin-zone parameter $k$ and counting windings of $(\langle\sigma_x\rangle,\langle\sigma_z\rangle)$ about the origin.

This correspondence was established for Hermitian, diagonalizable Hamiltonians. For non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that can be defective and have momentum-space exceptional points, it is unclear whether bulk invariants computed in a periodic geometry retain their predictive power for open geometries. conclusion.content:
Consider a one-dimensional tight-binding superlattice with M sites per unit cell, nearest-neighbor hopping amplitude J, and Bloch minibands indexed by l in the Hermitian limit (imaginary gauge field h = 0). Let the l-th intracell Hermitian eigenfunction at Bloch momentum k = 0 be denoted by $\phi_n^{(l)}$ (site index $n=1,\dots,M$) and suppose that this eigenfunction is tightly confined near the center of the unit cell and displays exponentially decaying evanescent tails with a characteristic decay rate (Lyapunov exponent / inverse localization length) $\gamma_{m}>0$ that does not shrink as $M$ increases. Let $\rho_{l}$ be the fraction of the $M$-site unit cell where $\phi_n^{(l)}$ is evanescent, with $0\lt \rho_{l}\leq 1$. Define the full bandwidth of the l-th miniband at $h=0$ to be $2\Delta_{l}$. In this regime, first-order perturbation theory in the weak inter-unit-cell boundary coupling (the matrix elements connecting sites $n=1$ and $n=M$) gives a leading $k$-dependent energy correction $E^{(1)}(k)=2J\cos(kM)\,\phi_1^{(l)}\phi_M^{(l)}$, and the miniband half-width satisfies $\Delta_{l}=-2J\,\phi_1^{(l)}\phi_M^{(l)}$. Because the boundary amplitudes scale as $\phi_1^{(l)}\phi_M^{(l)}\sim\exp(-\sigma_{l}M)$ with $\sigma_{l}=\rho_{l}\gamma_{m}$, the half-bandwidth thus scales as
      $$
      \Delta_{l}\sim\exp(-\sigma_{l}M),\qquad \sigma_{l}=\rho_{l}\gamma_{m},
      $$
      where $\gamma_{m}$ is the decay rate of the evanescent tails and $\rho_{l}$ is the evanescent-fraction of the unit cell (for example, $\rho_{l}=1$ for eigenstates exponentially localized over the whole unit cell as in Aubry–André–type incommensurate states, and $\rho_{l}=1/2$ for the alternating rectangular‑barrier example). This exponential-in-$M$ miniband narrowing follows from treating the inter-unit-cell boundary hoppings as a small perturbation and is confirmed by numerical calculations for the model superlattices described above.

Treating $\mathcal{H}_1(k)$ as a small perturbation on $\mathcal{H}_0$, the first‑order perturbative correction to the miniband energy associated with the normalized intracell eigenfunction $\phi_n^{(0)}$ is
      $$
      E^{(1)}(k)=\langle\phi^{(0)}|\mathcal{H}_1(k)|\phi^{(0)}\rangle=2J\cos(kM)\,\phi_1^{(0)}\phi_M^{(0)},
      $$
      hence the $k$-dependence of a near‑flat miniband is dominated by the single harmonic $\cos(kM)$ and higher harmonics or multi‑path tunneling contributions are negligible in the large‑$M$ near‑flat regime.

steps.reasoning: Define the one-dimensional tight-binding superlattice model with $M$ sites per unit cell and periodic boundary conditions: the Bloch Hamiltonian is the $M\times M$ matrix $\mathcal{H}(k)$ with real on-site potentials $V_n$ ($n=1,\dots,M$), nearest-neighbor real hopping amplitude $J$ between sites $n$ and $n\pm1$ inside the unit cell, and boundary hopping terms that couple site $1$ and site $M$ across the unit-cell boundary with phase factors $\exp(\pm i k M)$ induced by the Bloch wave number $k$ (the Bloch wave number $k$ varies in the interval $(-\pi/M,\pi/M)$). The non-Hermitian imaginary gauge field $h$ enters the full non-Hermitian problem by replacing $J\to J\exp(\pm h)$ for right/left hoppings, but the Hermitian limit of interest here is $h=0$ so that all hoppings equal $J$.

Introduce the $l$-th miniband eigenstate at $k=0$: denote by $\phi_n^{(l)}$ the components ($n=1,\dots,M$) of the $l$-th normalized eigenvector of $\mathcal{H}(k)$ at $k=0$, with Hermitian eigenenergy $E_l(0,0)$. Impose the normalization $\sum_{n=1}^{M}(\phi_n^{(l)})^{2}=1$ and assume, as the near-flat-band hypothesis, that $\phi_n^{(l)}$ is tightly confined near the center of the unit cell and exhibits exponentially-decaying tails near the unit-cell edges with a characteristic decay (Lyapunov) rate $\gamma_{m}>0$ that is independent of $M$ in the large-$M$ limit. Define explicitly the decay rate symbol: $\gamma_{m}$ is the inverse localization length of the intra-cell evanescent tails.

Define the fraction $\rho_{l}$ ($0<\rho_{l}\leq 1$) of the unit cell where the $l$-th intra-cell eigenfunction is evanescent: $\rho_{l}$ is the proportion (fraction) of the $M$ intracell sites over which $\phi_n^{(l)}$ displays exponential decay with rate $\gamma_{m}$. Examples: for an incommensurate/Aubry–André-type localized state one has $\rho_{l}=1$ (evanescent over the whole cell); for the rectangular-barrier example one has $\rho_{l}=1/2$ (evanescent over one half of the cell). This defines the combined exponent symbol $\sigma_{l}=\rho_{l}\gamma_{m}$ that will appear in the bandwidth scaling.

Decompose the Hermitian Bloch Hamiltonian at $h=0$ into a bulk tridiagonal part $\mathcal{H}_0$ (containing $J$ hoppings inside the cell and the on-site potentials $V_n$) and a boundary perturbation $\mathcal{H}_1(k)$ that contains only the two matrix elements coupling site $1$ and site $M$, which are $J\exp(-i k M)$ and its Hermitian conjugate $J\exp(i k M)$: $\mathcal{H}(k)=\mathcal{H}_0+\mathcal{H}_1(k)$. This split treats the boundary coupling as a small perturbation when the intra-cell eigenfunctions are exponentially small at the edges of the unit cell.

Apply non-degenerate perturbation theory for the $l$-th eigenstate in the small parameter given by the weakness of the boundary matrix elements (smallness follows from exponential vanishing of $\phi_1^{(l)}$ and $\phi_M^{(l)}$ with $M$): expand the eigenfunction and eigenenergy as $\phi^{(l)}(k)=\phi^{(l)(0)}+\phi^{(l)(1)}(k)+\dots$ and $E_l(k,0)=E^{(0)}+E^{(1)}(k)+\dots$, where $\phi^{(l)(0)}$ and $E^{(0)}$ are the $k=0$ eigenvector and eigenvalue of $\mathcal{H}_0$. The solvability condition at first order yields an explicit first-order energy correction.

Write the first-order energy correction for the $l$-th miniband as the matrix element of the perturbation between zeroth-order eigenstates:
$E^{(1)}(k)=\langle\phi^{(l)(0)}|\mathcal{H}_1(k)|\phi^{(l)(0)}\rangle=2J\cos(kM)\,\phi^{(l)(0)}_{1}\phi^{(l)(0)}_{M}$,
where $\phi^{(l)(0)}_{1}$ and $\phi^{(l)(0)}_{M}$ are the edge amplitudes of the zeroth-order eigenvector (these amplitudes are real under the chosen gauge for the Hermitian matrix). This step reproduces the perturbative solvability condition derived from the eigenvalue equation at first order.

Express the Hermitian miniband dispersion at leading order in the small boundary-coupling parameter as
$E_l(k,0)\simeq E_l(0,0)+\Delta_{l}[1-\cos(kM)]$,
where the single-miniband half-bandwidth parameter $\Delta_{l}$ is defined by
$\Delta_{l}=-2J\,\phi^{(l)(0)}_{1}\phi^{(l)(0)}_{M}$,
so that the full bandwidth (peak-to-trough) is $2\Delta_{l}$. This relation follows by regrouping the constant part $2J\phi_1^{(0)}\phi_M^{(0)}$ with $E^{(0)}$ and by identifying $\Delta_{l}$ from the first-order correction proportional to $\cos(kM)$.

Estimate the asymptotic $M$-dependence of the product of edge amplitudes $\phi^{(l)(0)}_{1}\phi^{(l)(0)}_{M}$ under the hypothesis that the wave function decays exponentially with rate $\gamma_{m}$ over a fraction $\rho_{l}$ of the unit cell: the dominant $M$-scaling is
$\phi^{(l)(0)}_{1}\phi^{(l)(0)}_{M}\sim\exp(-\sigma_{l}M)$,
where $\sigma_{l}=\rho_{l}\gamma_{m}$. The reasoning is: each evanescent stretch of length proportional to $\rho_{l}M$ attenuates amplitudes by $\sim\exp(-\gamma_{m}\times \text{length})$, so the product of the two edge amplitudes picks up a factor $\exp(-\rho_{l}\gamma_{m}M)$ in the large-$M$ limit. Reference illustration: the two paradigmatic cases in the main text are (i) the incommensurate Aubry–André-type superlattice where $\rho_{l}=1$ (evanescent over the whole cell) and (ii) the rectangular-barrier ordered superlattice where $\rho_{l}=1/2$ (evanescent over half the cell); these are illustrated in the schematics of the intra-cell wave functions. Fig.3

Combine the expressions for $\Delta_{l}$ and the exponential estimate of the edge-amplitude product to obtain the asymptotic bandwidth scaling in the Hermitian limit ($h=0$):
$\Delta_{l}\sim\exp(-\sigma_{l}M),\qquad \sigma_{l}=\rho_{l}\,\gamma_{m}$,
so that the full $l$-th miniband width $2\Delta_{l}$ vanishes exponentially with $M$ at rate $\sigma_{l}$. This is the stated miniband narrowing (near-flat-band) law derived perturbatively from the weak boundary coupling. Numerical illustrations of this exponential-in-$M$ miniband narrowing for the model superlattices are provided in the main text figures. Fig.4(a)Fig.5(a)

motivating_questions.content: Physical/scientific context: In a periodic superlattice with many intracell sites $M$, the Bloch minibands at $h=0$ can become very narrow (near-flat) when intra-cell eigenfunctions have evanescent tails that overlap weakly across the unit-cell boundary. Prior state of knowledge: Earlier studies used superlattices to approximate quasicrystals or disordered systems but did not present a general, quantitative large-$M$ scaling law linking the miniband width to the intra-cell decay properties and the fraction of the cell occupied by evanescent tails. Shortcomings of prior approaches: Without a clear scaling relation, one cannot predict how rapidly minibands flatten as $M$ grows or determine the sensitivity of the spectrum to a non-Hermitian complexification of momentum. Scientific consequences of the gap: Lacking this scaling prevents precise prediction of whether a superlattice will display an abrupt spectral deformation as an imaginary gauge field is tuned, and it prevents mapping between the superlattice limit and the delocalization physics known in disordered NH models.

steps.reasoning:
We consider a general tight-binding non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in d spatial dimensions with open boundary conditions along x and periodic boundary conditions along the remaining (d-1) directions parametrized by transverse quasimomentum k_perp. The Hamiltonian has the form
H = sum_n sum_{alpha,beta=1}^q [ sum_{ell=1}^R (c_{n,alpha}^dagger [t_{L,ell}]_{alpha,beta} c_{n+ell,beta} + c_{n+ell,alpha}^dagger [t_{R,ell}^dagger]_{alpha,beta} c_{n,beta}) + c_{n,alpha}^dagger [t_0]_{alpha,beta} c_{n,beta} ]
where t_{L,ell} and t_{R,ell} are hopping matrices to left and right respectively, t_0 is the intra-unit-cell term, and q internal degrees of freedom per unit cell. The hopping range R is finite.

By bundling together n >= qR degrees of freedom into a supercell (with creation operators c_n^dagger), the Hamiltonian reduces to nearest-neighbor form:
H(k_perp) = sum_{n=0}^N [ c_n^dagger J_L c_{n+1} + c_n^dagger M c_n + c_{n+1}^dagger J_R^dagger c_n ]
with hopping matrices J_{L,R} and onsite matrix M.

The single-particle Schrodinger equation H|Psi> = epsilon |Psi> with |Psi> = sum_n Psi_n c_n^dagger |Omega> yields the recursion relation:
J_L Psi_{n+1} + M Psi_n + J_R^dagger Psi_{n-1} = epsilon Psi_n
We specialize to the case where J_R = J_L = J and J^2 = 0. The condition J^2=0 can always be satisfied by choosing a sufficiently large supercell; it ensures that the singular vectors of J form an orthonormal set. Under these assumptions, the recursion becomes:
J Psi_{n+1} + M Psi_n + J^dagger Psi_{n-1} = epsilon Psi_n

We rewrite the recursion relation by introducing the onsite Green's function G = (epsilon 1 - M)^{-1}, which is non-singular except when epsilon is an eigenvalue of M. This gives:
Psi_n = G J Psi_{n+1} + G J^dagger Psi_{n-1}

We compute a reduced singular value decomposition of J:
J = V Xi W^dagger
where Xi = diag{xi_1, ..., xi_r} with r = rank J, and the singular values xi_i > 0. The r left and right singular vectors are assembled in the n x r matrices V and W, which satisfy:
V^dagger V = W^dagger W = 1_r,  V^dagger W = 0
The orthogonality V^dagger W = 0 follows from J^2 = 0, which also ensures r <= n/2.

We rearrange these equations into a transfer matrix form. Define the vector:
Phi_n = (beta_n, alpha_{n-1})^T
The system can be written as:
Phi_{n+1} = T Phi_n
where the 2r-dimensional transfer matrix is:
T = [ [ Xi^{-1} G_vw^{-1},  -Xi^{-1} G_vw^{-1} G_ww Xi ];  [ G_vv G_vw^{-1},  (G_ww - G_vv G_vw^{-1} G_ww) Xi ] ]

The determinant of T is computed as:
det T = det( G_vw^{-1} G_wv ) = det G_wv / det G_vw
Thus det T depends on the ratio of determinants of the projected Green's functions.

For non-Hermitian systems, a distinct possibility is |det T| -> 0 or infinity when |det G_wv| -> 0 or |det G_vw| -> 0. These correspond to unidirectionality in the system, since states can then be propagated only in one direction. The construction also yields a transfer matrix for left eigenstates by considering H^dagger.
[76]

motivating_questions.content: To study non-Hermitian topological phases analytically, one needs a real-space method that can handle both periodic and open boundary conditions on equal footing. Transfer matrices are a natural tool for Hermitian tight-binding chains, but their generalization to non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, where the hopping matrices may be singular and the recursion relations involve both left and right hoppings, requires a careful construction that respects the nilpotence condition $J^2=0$ (ensuring that singular vectors form an orthonormal set). Prior work on non-Hermitian systems relied heavily on numerical exact diagonalization or continuum approximations, lacking a systematic analytical framework for arbitrary lattice models. A transfer matrix formalism for non-Hermitian systems would provide the necessary foundation to derive spectral properties, wave functions, and topological invariants from a single object.

Define the spectral winding number $W(E)$ for a given complex energy $E\in\mathbb{C}$ on the compactified momentum circle $\tilde{k}\in[-\pi,\pi]$ by
$$
W(E)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{d\tilde{k}}{2\pi i}\frac{d}{d\tilde{k}}\log\det(\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_{\tilde{k}}(\tilde{k})-E),
$$
where $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_{\tilde{k}}(\tilde{k})$ denotes the dynamical matrix expressed as a function of the compactified momentum $\tilde{k}$ (i.e., with $k=\tan(\tilde{k})$), and the logarithm branch is chosen consistently so that the integral yields an integer; this definition follows the spectral winding-number construction used to classify non-Hermitian skin effects.

The spectrum and GBZ are obtained from the characteristic equation $f(\beta,E)=\det\left[H(\beta)-E\right]=0$, whose $2M$ roots in $\beta$ are ordered by modulus $|\beta_1|\le\ldots\le|\beta_{2M}|$. The continuum-band (open-chain) condition is
$$
|\beta_M|=|\beta_{M+1}|,
$$
and the generalized Brillouin zone $C_\beta$ is given by the trajectories of $\beta_M$ and $\beta_{M+1}$ in the complex-$\beta$ plane. Under this formalism $H(\beta)$ evaluated on $C_\beta$ reproduces spectra and eigenstates of the system under open-boundary conditions.

steps.reasoning: Define the complex variable $\beta$ by $\beta:=e^{ik}$, where $k$ is the (complexified) wave number; here $\beta$ is promoted from the unit circle of Bloch theory to the full complex plane to capture non-Hermitian effects.

Define the non-Bloch Hamiltonian $H(\beta)$ as the Hamiltonian obtained by substituting $\beta$ for $e^{ik}$ in the Bloch Hamiltonian; $H(\beta)$ is therefore a matrix-valued function of the complex variable $\beta$ and is used to describe the periodic (generalized) momentum dependence of a one-dimensional non-Hermitian superconductor.

Introduce the characteristic function $f(\beta,E)$ by $f(\beta,E)=\det\!\big[H(\beta)-E\big]$, where $E$ denotes a (complex) eigenvalue; the allowed pairs $(\beta,E)$ for the system satisfy the algebraic equation $f(\beta,E)=0$, which is an even-order polynomial equation in $\beta$ in generic superconducting models.

Label the $2M$ solutions in $\beta$ of the characteristic equation $f(\beta,E)=0$ (for fixed $E$) as $\beta_i$ with $i=1,2,\ldots,2M$, and order them by modulus so that $|\beta_1|\leq|\beta_2|\leq\ldots\leq|\beta_{2M}|$; here the integer $M$ equals half the order of the polynomial in $\beta$ and corresponds to the number of particle-hole pairs of roots inherited from the superconducting Bogoliubov structure.

State the continuum-band (open-chain) condition: the open-boundary continuum bands of the system arise from values of $\beta$ for which the $M$-th and $(M+1)$-th ordered roots have equal moduli, i.e. 
$\;|\beta_{M}|=|\beta_{M+1}|\,$; this condition identifies the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ) as the locus where the two middle-modulus solutions trade dominance and produce the continuum-spectrum relevant to an open chain. 
[7, 54, 60]

Define the generalized Brillouin zone $C_{\beta}$ as the trajectories in the complex-$\beta$ plane traced by $\beta_{M}$ and $\beta_{M+1}$ as $E$ varies along the continuum bands; explicitly, $C_{\beta}$ is given by the set of complex $\beta$ values that satisfy the continuum-band condition $|\beta_{M}|=|\beta_{M+1}|$.

Assert that evaluating the non-Bloch Hamiltonian $H(\beta)$ on the GBZ $C_{\beta}$ reproduces the spectra and eigenstates of the finite open chain under open-boundary conditions (OBC): the non-Bloch formulation therefore replaces Bloch theory for predicting OBC spectra in non-Hermitian superconductors, because the GBZ replaces the unit circle BZ used in Hermitian systems.

Reference the illustrative schematic of paired reciprocal GBZ loops and opposite-end eigenstate localization that accompanies the formulation to indicate how the GBZ and $H(\beta)$ reproduce open-chain features in concrete examples.

motivating_questions.content: In non-Hermitian one-dimensional lattices with nonreciprocal hopping, periodic-boundary (Bloch) spectra generally do not converge to open-boundary spectra because eigenstates can exhibit exponential spatial growth/decay and accumulate at boundaries. Prior superconducting studies often relied on Bloch Hamiltonians or computed open-boundary spectra model-by-model without a unifying prescription for how to choose complex wave numbers that reproduce the open-chain physics. Without a formal non-Bloch criterion for which complex $\beta$ produce continuum bands, one cannot systematically compute open-chain spectra, GBZ loops, or derive topology that predicts boundary Majorana modes. Establishing the ordering of $\beta$ roots and the continuum-band condition $|\beta_M|=|\beta_{M+1}|$ addresses this foundational gap and provides the correct kinematic space (the GBZ) for all subsequent non-Bloch spectral and topological analysis.

conclusion.content:
For bosonic Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) systems, the time-evolution of the bosonic field operators is governed by the $M(t)$ matrix,
      $$
      M(t) = \begin{pmatrix} h(t) & \Delta(t) \\ -\Delta^*(t) & -h^{\mathrm{T}}(t) \end{pmatrix},
      $$
      where $h(t)$ is the single-particle Hamiltonian and $\Delta(t)$ is the pairing term. The same generalized Bernard–LeClair (GBL) symmetry analysis and K-theory hermitianization procedures developed for fermionic Floquet non-Hermitian systems apply to $M(t)$. For example, the generic bosonic BdG symmetry places $M(t)$ in GBL class QC8a. Using the Floquet-operator (FO) angle-gapped periodic table (Table I) or the FO angle-gapless periodic table (Table II) for the corresponding GBL class yields the allowed strong topological invariants and their dimensional dependence for bosonic Floquet systems. Explicit driven bosonic honeycomb examples (two-dimensional) and reducible-block driven bosonic one-dimensional examples are constructed and shown to realize the predicted invariants and chiral lifetimes (spectral imaginary parts).

steps.reasoning: Begin from conclusion 1 (54 GBL classes) as known; introduce bosonic Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) dynamics and define the bosonic evolution generator: for bosonic creation/annihilation operators $\hat{a}_{i\mu}^{\dagger},\hat{a}_{i\mu}$ the quadratic BdG Hamiltonian is written in real-space tight-binding BdG form and the Heisenberg equation of motion for the Nambu-like column $(\hat{\Psi},\hat{\bar{\Psi}})^{\mathrm{T}}$ leads to a linear evolution equation $\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\Psi}\\\hat{\bar{\Psi}}\end{pmatrix}=-iM(t)\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\Psi}\\\hat{\bar{\Psi}}\end{pmatrix}$, where the $M(t)$ matrix (called the M matrix) is defined below.

Write the explicit expression for the bosonic BdG $M(t)$ matrix and define symbols: $h$ is the single-particle (possibly non-Hermitian) hopping/potential block, $\Delta$ is the pairing matrix (symmetric for bosons), and $\mathbf{T}$ denotes matrix transpose. The M matrix is
$$
M(t):=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta\\[4pt]-\Delta^{*}&-h^{\mathbf{T}}\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $\Delta_{i\mu,j\nu}=\Delta_{j\nu,i\mu}$ and indices $i,j$ label unit cells while $\mu,\nu$ label internal degrees of freedom.
(Here $\hat{\Psi}=(\hat{a}_{11},\ldots,\hat{a}_{Lm})^{\mathrm{T}}$ and $\hat{\bar{\Psi}}=(\hat{a}_{11}^{\dagger},\ldots,\hat{a}_{Lm}^{\dagger})^{\mathrm{T}}$.)

Observe that $M(t)$ plays the same role for bosons that $H(t)$ plays for fermions: $M(t)$ is a generally non-Hermitian, time-dependent generator of linear evolution and hence the group-structure symmetry analysis and topological classification framework developed for time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonians carry over to $M(t)$ after identifying the internal-symmetry operations appropriate to $M(t)$.

Identify the specific GBL class assignment for the generic bosonic BdG M matrix under the natural particle–hole / BdG constraints: for a Hermitian bosonic BdG Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_b$ with pairing, $M(t)$ satisfies the relations corresponding to three (matrix) symmetries (using Pauli-like $\tau$ matrices acting in particle-hole/Nambu space): $\tau_x M(t)\tau_x = -M^{*}(t)$, $\tau_z M(t)\tau_z = M^{\dagger}(t)$, and $\tau_y M(t)\tau_y = -M^{\mathbf{T}}(t)$. From these relations the authors identify the generic bosonic BdG $M(t)$ as belonging to the GBL class labeled QC8a (i.e., it carries both a Q-type and a C-type structure with the sign choices corresponding to class QC8a).

Invoke the classification machinery already developed for fermionic FNH systems (the two periodic tables for FO angle-gapped and FO angle-gapless cases) and apply it to $M(t)$ by treating $M(t)$ as the time-dependent non-Hermitian operator to hermitianize and to subject to the Clifford-algebra / K-theory extension procedure; explicitly, for FO angle-gapped bosonic M matrices one uses the loop-operator hermitianization $\tilde H(\mathbf{k},t)=\begin{pmatrix}0&U_{l,\pi}(\mathbf{k},t)\\U_{l,\pi}(\mathbf{k},t)^\dagger&0\end{pmatrix}$ (for the loop) and $H_{F,\pi}$ for the Floquet Hamiltonian; for FO angle-gapless bosonic M matrices one uses $\bar H(\mathbf{k})=\begin{pmatrix}0&U(\mathbf{k})\\U(\mathbf{k})^\dagger&0\end{pmatrix}$, exactly as in the fermionic case, with the transformed GBL symmetry relations appropriate to $M(t)$. The class assignment QC8a determines which classifying space ($C_n$ or $R_m$, possibly with multiplicities) is used and hence the topological invariant groups follow from Table I / Table II entries corresponding to QC8a.
Fig. 5

Extract the concrete invariant predictions for bosonic BdG Floquet systems in QC8a from the periodic tables as given by the authors: for FO angle-gapped bosonic $M(t)$ in QC8a the FO angle-gapped periodic table (Table I) yields strong invariants $ \mathbb{Z}^{n_p}$ in even spatial dimensions and $0$ in odd dimensions, where $n_p$ counts relevant FO angle gaps (e.g., $n_p=1$ if only a single FO angle gap at $0$ or $\pi$, $n_p=2$ if both $0$ and $\pi$ gaps exist); for FO angle-gapless bosonic $M(t)$ the FO angle-gapless periodic table (Table II) yields $0$ in even dimensions and $\mathbb{Z}$ in odd dimensions for QC8a, as summarized in the paper.

Note that the authors constructed explicit driven bosonic examples (a driven bosonic honeycomb with pairing and a reducible-block driven 1D bosonic example) whose M-matrix Floquet operators realize the predicted invariants and show the corresponding edge phenomena and complex quasienergy imaginary parts ("chiral lifetimes"); the spectra and winding numbers for these examples (figures and numerical values) are described in the examples section and the figures in the paper demonstrate the realization of the predicted bosonic invariants.

steps.reasoning: A one-dimensional topological insulator with lattice translational symmetry is usually described by a Bloch wave $\psi(x)=e^{ikx}u(x)$, where $x$ is the lattice coordinate, $k$ is the Bloch wave number, and $u(x)$ is the periodic part satisfying $u(x+1)=u(x)$.

For a finite system, the standard periodic boundary condition $\psi(x+L)=\psi(x)$ forces the Bloch factor $\beta$ in the generalized form $\psi(x)=\beta^{x}u(x)$ to satisfy $\beta^{L}=1$, so that $|\beta|=1$ and the allowed states lie on the unit circle in the complex $\beta$ plane.

In non-Hermitian systems with non-reciprocal hopping, the open-boundary eigenwave function is not generically of the plane-wave form; instead it is a generalized Bloch wave $\psi(x)=\beta^{x}u(x)$ with $|\beta|\neq 1$ possible, and such a wave can exponentially damp or amplify, producing the non-Hermitian skin effect.

The paper states that the periodic-boundary bulk spectrum in such non-Hermitian examples fails to reproduce the open-boundary gap closings and boundary-state structure, so the standard Bloch band theory under the usual periodic closure is not a correct bulk description.

To remedy this, a modified periodic boundary condition is introduced in the form $\psi(x+L)=b^{L}\psi(x)$ with $b$ a real positive constant. This relaxes the closure condition so that the allowed Bloch factors satisfy $\beta^{L}=b^{L}$, i.e. $|\beta|=b$ and $\beta=b e^{ik}$.

Because the generalized Bloch factor is no longer restricted to the unit circle, the modified periodic boundary condition supplies a generalized bulk geometry that can be tuned to remain consistent with the open-boundary problem and thus restore a meaningful bulk description for the non-Hermitian system.

motivating_questions.content: In non-Hermitian one-dimensional topological systems with non-reciprocal hopping, the usual periodic boundary condition forces Bloch factors onto the unit circle and therefore inherits the standard Hermitian notion of bulk states, but this is precisely where the non-Hermitian skin effect makes the ordinary Bloch description unreliable. Under open boundaries, bulk eigenstates are generically not plane waves but exponentially damped or amplified generalized Bloch waves, so the spectrum and gap closings seen in the boundary geometry do not match those obtained from the standard periodic bulk band. A proper bulk description is therefore needed in which the closure of the finite system is not overly restrictive and can accommodate non-unit-modulus Bloch factors, so that bulk quantities remain meaningful and can be related one-to-one to the open-boundary spectrum and boundary states.
